want.now.why: vouloir takes a bare infinitive: no 'to', no que. Language names keep their article, so the object is le khasi, not khasi.

want.past.why: Tense sits inside the door: voulais is the imparfait, the natural past for a wish. j'ai voulu (passé composé) would mean I tried to.

want.neg.why: Negation is two pieces that wrap the door: ne before veux, pas after it and before the infinitive. Speech drops ne: je veux pas apprendre.

want.q.why: No question word at all: statement order, rising pitch, and a space before the ? as French writes it. Est-ce que tu veux... is the other spoken option.

decline.now.why: parce que does nothing to the second clause: same subject-door-verb order as a main clause. Speech: je peux pas venir, parce que je dois bosser.

decline.past.why: The failed attempt is passé composé, so pas slips between ai and pu; the standing obligation stays imparfait (devais). Speech: j'ai pas pu venir.

decline.fut.why: Futur proche: vais carries the tense and ne ... pas wraps it, while pouvoir and devoir stay infinitives. je pourrai pas / je devrai is the futur simple alternative.

decline.although.why: Spoken French prefers même si + indicative here. The textbook glue bien que would force the subjunctive: bien que je doive travailler.

like.now.why: je loses its e before a vowel and becomes j'. The liked thing takes the definite article: le café means coffee in general, not a cup.

like.neg.why: ne elides to n' before aime; pas follows the door. Speech drops n' entirely: j'aime pas le café. The article stays le after aimer, unlike du after a negated verb.

like.she.why: aime is spelled and sounds the same as for je: the person is heard only in the pronoun elle, not in the verb ending.

like.q.why: est-ce que is a frozen question opener: after it the order is plain statement order. Tu aimes le café ? with rising pitch is equally common.

go.habit.why: à + le fuses into au: au marché is one unit. The time phrase follows the destination, as in English; putting it first is also fine.

go.prog.why: No progressive: je vais is both I go and I am going, so là (right now) does all the work. je suis en train d'aller exists but is heavy for a trip.

go.past.why: aller takes être, not avoir, in the passé composé, and the participle agrees with the speaker: allé for a man, allée for a woman, same sound.

go.fut.why: Futur simple on an irregular stem: ir- + -ai. Tense is a suffix, not a separate word. Plain present with demain (je vais au marché demain) is just as spoken.

go.neg.why: No auxiliary and no -ing: ne ... pas wraps the plain present vais. Speech: je vais pas au marché.

live.now.why: Present tense plus depuis: no perfect, no auxiliary. habite is the same form as in I live here; depuis alone says it started in the past and continues.

live.past.why: Finished period, so passé composé with avoir, and the duration switches from depuis to pendant. In speech pendant is often dropped: j'ai habité là-bas deux ans.

live.fut.why: Not a future perfect: the future goes onto ça fera (it will make), the duration follows, que links, and habiter stays present. j'aurai habité sounds written.

live.q.why: The question phrase stays in place at the end, where depuis deux ans would be, and the verb is plain present. Depuis combien de temps tu habites ici ? also works.

if.real.why: si + present, futur simple in the main clause: the -rai ending is the whole of English will. je vais voyager or plain je voyage are also heard.

if.unreal.why: si + imparfait (avais), conditionnel (voyagerais) in the main clause. Never si + conditionnel: the schoolroom rule is les si n'aiment pas les -rais.

if.past.why: Both clauses are avoir + participle: plus-que-parfait (avais eu) after si, conditionnel passé (aurais voyagé) in the main. Only the tense of avoir changes.
